summary: Describes high-level requirements for Internet Voice Mail, extending VPIM version 2 to work with desktop clients and unified messaging. It sets a baseline against which proposed MIME profiles for voice messaging can be judged. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Voice messages should travel like email. This lists what a system must do so voice mail from phones and computers works together.

questions: how should voice mail systems interoperate
what formats should voice mail use
subtitle: What voice mail systems must do to work together over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Voice mail systems have been proprietary stand-alone systems. As desktop computers become as common as telephones, systems need to work together, supporting voice messages alongside email on both phones and computers.
tldr.mechanism: Internet Voice Mail (IVM) defines requirements for systems to exchange voice messages using Internet standards: SMTP for transport, MIME for message structure, and support for both traditional voice mail systems and email clients.
tldr.outcome: IVM allows voice messages to flow between voice mail systems, unified messaging systems, email servers, and desktop applications, while maintaining backward compatibility with earlier VPIM systems.

today: RFC 3773 is an Informational RFC published in June 2004 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the baseline requirements document for Internet Voice Mail systems.

sections.title: Voice Mail Moves to the Internet
sections.content:
RFC 3773 defines high-level requirements for Internet Voice Mail (IVM), a profile that extends the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) version 2. Traditionally, voice mail was handled by stand-alone systems connected to telephone switches. Today, with computers ubiquitous in offices and homes, voice messages need to integrate with email systems and desktop applications.

IVM specifies how voice mail systems, unified messaging systems (which combine voicemail, email, and fax), email servers, and desktop email clients should work together. The goal is to let a user listen to voice messages from their phone, desktop, web browser, or even reply with a voice message from their computer—regardless of what system their contact uses.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice mail and email are merging. This explains what systems need to do so voice messages work as smoothly as text messages between different computers and phones.

sections.title: Making Different Systems Talk
sections.content:
The primary goal of IVM is enhanced interoperability. An IVM-compliant message sent from one system should arrive intact at its destination, even if the sender and receiver use different platforms.

IVM defines interoperability with four key system types: desktop email clients (like Outlook or Thunderbird), IVM-capable voice mail systems, unified messaging systems, and traditional email servers that handle only text. The RFC requires that essential message parts be preserved, status codes understood, and standard operations supported.

A critical concern is backward compatibility with VPIM version 2 systems already deployed. IVM systems may need to handle codecs (audio compression methods) from earlier versions, and must gracefully handle recipients that cannot process IVM-specific audio formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Different systems need to understand each other, like mail carriers from different countries. The document says what each type of system must be able to do.

sections.title: Technical and Format Requirements
sections.content:
IVM specifies several technical constraints. Voice content must be carried in standard audio formats; at minimum, at least one mandatory codec must be widely available on desktop computers. The RFC names codec criteria: they should be available on most platforms, have readily accessible source code, be low-complexity to decode, and support Voice over IP (VoIP) implementations.

Messages may contain multiple media types (voice, text, fax). Clients must support attachments of any media type and allow text body parts in voice messages. The RFC requires a mechanism to describe message content so devices can indicate how content can be accessed—important for devices that cannot handle specific formats.

IVM must work through legacy gateways that do not understand MIME, and must handle recipients with limited buffering. It must support authenticated and encrypted voice messages and follow security practices from SMTP, Internet Message Format, and MIME standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice needs to be recorded in a common format so any computer can play it. Messages can mix voice, text, and pictures, and every system needs to tell the others what it can handle.

sections.title: Staying Compatible with Existing Standards
sections.content:
IVM aims to impose as few restrictions as possible on existing Internet mail standards. It must support all elements of RFC 2822 (Internet Message Format) except where those elements conflict with other IVM goals. The profile should make minimal additions to standards; where new MIME types are needed, they should use terms already standard in desktop environments.

Another goal is backward compatibility with VPIM version 2. Where full backward compatibility cannot be achieved, IVM defines status codes and rules for handling non-delivery when interoperating with legacy systems. The RFC emphasizes that IVM must be usable in environments where legacy gateways do not understand MIME, and that core features and critical data must not be lost in such cases.
sections.plainLanguage: New systems should follow the old rules when possible, so older voice mail boxes still work. When they can't, the system explains the problem clearly.

sections.title: Why Voice Mail Needs These Standards
sections.content:
The shift from stand-alone voice mail systems to integrated messaging demands clear requirements. Users expect voice messages to arrive just as reliably as text, and to be accessible from multiple devices. Businesses deploying unified messaging need to know what interoperability they can count on.

IVM provides that baseline. By defining mandatory features, optional features, codec choices, and security practices, the specification allows independent implementations to work together. The focus on desktop clients and email integration reflects the reality that voice mail is no longer a separate service—it is part of the communication mix that includes text, images, and video.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice mail is now part of email. Everyone needs to know what features are required, what is optional, and how to handle problems so the system is reliable.
